query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing chemical short-range order (SRO) in as-cast HfNbTaTiZr HEA by tailored intermediate annealing treatments will increase the alloy’s elastic stiffness and yield strength, reduce dislocation mobility during plastic deformation, and lower its thermal expansion coefficient at elevated temperatures compared to a rapidly quenched (near-random) baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA with minimal SRO (rapidly quenched)
generation.intervention: Subject samples to intermediate annealing treatments (800–1100 K) for controlled durations followed by rapid quenching to promote the formation of SRO
generation.conditions: Testing performed in situ using high-temperature tensile tests and nanoindentation between 673 K and 1273 K
generation.structural_mediator: Increased chemical short-range order that introduces additional dislocation pinning sites
generation.mechanism: The annealing process promotes local atomic rearrangements, increasing SRO. The enhanced SRO modifies the local bonding environment, thereby stiffening the material and raising the yield strength. It also impedes dislocation nucleation and mobility, leading to reduced plastic relaxation and a decrease in the thermal expansion coefficient due to more rigid local interactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline rapidly quenched alloy, the SRO-enhanced samples will exhibit higher elastic modulus and yield strength, diminished plastic deformation (evidenced by greater residual dislocation density post-indentation), and a reduced thermal expansion coefficient within the 673–1273 K testing range.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with minimal SRO
generation.boundary: Valid for HfNbTaTiZr HEA within the temperature range of 673 K to 1273 K, using annealing treatments between 800 K and 1100 K
generation.uncertainty: The precision in controlling and quantitatively measuring the degree of SRO poses experimental challenges, which may obscure clear correlations between SRO levels and the predicted mechanical and thermal properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set is rapidly quenched to retain a near-random atomic distribution (baseline), and the other set undergoes annealing treatments at 800–1100 K for various durations followed by rapid quenching to enhance SRO. Conduct in situ high-temperature tensile tests and nanoindentation experiments within the temperature range of 673–1273 K.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SRO-enhanced samples do not systematically show higher stiffness and yield strength, reduced plastic deformation (i.e., higher residual dislocation density), and lower thermal expansion compared to the rapidly quenched baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). The mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys are receiving continuous attention as they combine excellent strength with ductility,. One of the microscopic origins of their features lies in the slow dislocation activity in these alloys, that is caused by the lattice distortion brought about by the mix of atomic constituents with various sizes. Recently, high-entropy alloys forming single-phase bcc crystals have come into the focus of research. Among them, the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy has become one of the best investigated examples; it is also known as the Senkov alloy. Thus, Xu et al. directly model the shear strength of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy and observe failure by a bcc-to-fcc phase transformation initiating in HfTi rich regions. Liang et al. study how variable fractions of Hf and Ta in HfNbTaTiZr alloys affect the tensile strength. Recently, Hf15Nb40Ta25Ti15Zr15 was found to be both strong and ductile at cryogenic to elevated temperatures. Due to the chemical complexity of these concentrated alloys, the local stoichiometry may deviate from the overall composition leading to local chemical short-range order. We note that in previous studies, the influence of short-range order on the hardness of the medium-entropy fcc alloy CoCrNi was studied. Experimentally, larger hardness and strength are found for the short-range-ordered alloy than for the random alloy. This fact is corroborated by dedicated simulations of the behavior under nanoindentation,, where it is found that with increasing short-range order, indentation hardness and strength increase. This strengthening behavior was attributed to an increase of the force needed for dislocation nucleation; also, dislocation pinning was increased by local Ni short-range-ordered structures. The effects found for the fcc alloy thus parallel closely those found in the present study for the bcc HEA.

We explored the mechanical properties of the high-entropy bcc Senkov alloy by simulated nanoindentation. Both a random HfNbTaTiZr alloy and an alloy exhibiting short-range order were modeled and their performance was compared to that of an elementary Ta crystal. The simulation volume was chosen sufficiently large (> 20 million atoms) that boundary effects were minimized. Short-range order was introduced into the sample by a Monte Carlo procedure. We observe a slight stiffening of the elastic constants and an increase of the indentation hardness on the 10% level. These changes are caused by the generation of HfTi-rich precipitates in the B2 structure which impede dislocation motion and help hardening. The existence of such precipitates is in line with previous work. The indentation-induced plasticity is mainly based on dislocation generation and activation. However, dislocation emission from the plastic zone under the indenter, which is a common phenomenon in elemental bcc crystals and also in Ta, is strongly impeded or even absent in the alloys. Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. AbstractThe solid state phase transformation kinetics of as-cast and cold rolling deformed Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys have been investigated by the thermal expansion method. The phase transformed volume fractions are determined from the thermal expansion curve using the lever rule method, and the deformed sample exhibits a much higher transformation rate. Two kinetic parameters, activation energy (E) and kinetic exponent (n) are determined using Kissinger– Akahira–Sunose (KAS) and Johnson–Mehl–Avrami (JMA) method, respectively. Results show that a pre-deformed sample shows a much lower activation energy and higher kinetic exponent compared with the as-cast sample, which are interpreted based on the deformation induced defects that can promote the nucleation and growth process during phase transformation.Keywords: high-entropy alloy, phase transformation, kinetics, deformation, thermal expansion

The effects of cold rolling on the phase transformation kinetics of an Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy are studied by the thermal expansion method. The transformed volume fraction–temperature curves of as-cast and 20% cold rolling Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys are determined by the lever rule method using thermal expansion curves. Using the KAS method, the mean activation energy for as-cast and deformed HEAs calculated are 181 kJ/mol and 159 kJ/mol, respectively. The kinetic exponent is determined using the local Avrami exponent method based on the JMA equation. Both as-cast and deformed samples show the three stages of kinetic exponent variations, and the deformed alloy shows a much larger value compared with the as-cast alloy, indicating a much higher nucleation and growth rate. The reason for the kinetic exponent variations are thought to be related with the deformation induced strain and defects inside the sample that can generate a much higher energy that favors the nucleation and growth process.

proposals.material_system: HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) in as-cast form
proposals.intervention: Tailored heat treatments to control the degree of chemical short-range order (SRO)
proposals.conditions: Systematically anneal samples at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 800–1100 K) for varying durations followed by rapid quenching; perform in situ high-temperature tensile and nanoindentation tests between 673 K and 1273 K
proposals.structural_mediator: Degree of chemical short-range order and associated dislocation pinning sites
proposals.mechanism: Enhanced SRO is expected to alter the local bonding environment, thereby increasing elastic moduli and yield strength while potentially modifying the thermal expansion coefficient due to anisotropic atomic interactions. Modified SRO influences dislocation nucleation and mobility during plastic deformation, leading to a changed stress–strain response.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline (rapidly quenched, near-random alloy), the SRO-enhanced samples will display increased stiffness and yield strength, diminished plastic relaxation under nanoindentation (i.e., larger residual dislocation densities), and possibly reduced thermal expansion due to more rigid local structures. A clear falsification criterion would be if varying the annealing treatment does not yield systematic changes in elastic or thermal expansion behavior at elevated temperatures.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It directly tests whether microstructural ordering (a known factor in HEAs) is responsible for anomalous stress–strain behavior, elastic anisotropy, and thermal expansion at high temperatures in HfNbTaTiZr.

proposals.material_system: HfNbTaTiZr HEA in cold-rolled and annealed states
proposals.intervention: Introduce controlled plastic deformation via cold rolling followed by partial annealing to adjust dislocation densities
proposals.conditions: Prepare two sample sets: one as-cast (baseline) and one cold-rolled to ~20% thickness reduction followed by annealing at 900–1000 K to stabilize defect structures; perform tensile tests and thermal expansion measurements from 673 K to 1073 K
proposals.structural_mediator: Dislocation density and distribution of deformation-induced defects
proposals.mechanism: High dislocation densities and defect clusters from cold deformation can enhance short-range atomic rearrangements during heating. These defects could either act as nucleation sites for thermal expansion-relieving events or impede dislocation mobility at high temperatures, thereby affecting the stress–strain response and elastic moduli.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline as-cast alloy, the deformed and annealed alloy should show altered yield strength (potentially elevated due to dislocation pinning) accompanied by a modified thermal expansion profile. If the hypothesis is correct, the test would be falsified if no significant differences appear between the two processing routes within the defined temperature window.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It explores the role of deformation-induced defects in modulating high-temperature mechanical responses, thereby offering insight into the interplay between microstructural defects and intrinsic elastic/thermal properties.

proposals.material_system: HfNbTaTiZr HEA modeled as both random solid solution and with imposed short-range order
proposals.intervention: Atomistic simulations (molecular dynamics) contrasting two variants: one with a random atomic arrangement and one with artificially imposed SRO
proposals.conditions: Set up large-scale MD simulations (>20 million atoms if possible) to mimic nanoindentation and uniaxial tensile loading at elevated temperatures (e.g., 673–1273 K); use established EAM potentials validated on similar HEAs
proposals.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale chemical ordering and its effect on dislocation nucleation and mobility
proposals.mechanism: Imposing chemical SRO is predicted to increase the alloy’s local stiffness and hinder dislocation glide due to stronger local bonding, resulting in a distinct plastic zone morphology and modified thermal expansion behavior compared to the random alloy; this directly influences stress–strain responses.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The simulations should show that the SRO-containing alloy exhibits higher elastic moduli and yield strength, with larger but more static plastic zones resulting in limited strain recovery upon unloading. A falsification criterion would be if simulation results show no discernible difference in mechanical or thermal behavior between SRO and random structures.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It provides mechanistic insight at the atomic level, linking observed high-temperature stress–strain, elastic, and thermal expansion phenomena to the presence of short-range order, thereby explaining response differences in the HEA.

proposals.material_system: HfNbTaTiZr HEA produced with engineered grain sizes (nanostructured vs. coarse-grained)
proposals.intervention: Grain boundary engineering through controlled processing (e.g., spark plasma sintering followed by appropriate heat treatments) to produce variants with significantly different grain sizes
proposals.conditions: Fabricate samples with nanocrystalline (~100 nm) and coarse-grained (> 10 μm) microstructures; test stress–strain behavior, elastic moduli, and thermal expansion at high temperatures ranging from 673 K to 1273 K using in situ high-temperature mechanical testing and dilatometry
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain size and grain boundary density
proposals.mechanism: Grain boundaries can act as barriers to dislocation movement and sites for enhanced diffusion. In nanostructured alloys, high grain boundary density may lead to increased stiffening at elevated temperatures due to suppressed dislocation mobility and modified thermal expansion due to boundary contributions. The contrasting behavior with coarse grains tests the role of mesoscopic architecture in dictating the overall mechanical response.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The nanostructured samples are anticipated to exhibit higher yield strength and altered thermal expansion coefficients (likely a reduced overall expansion) compared to the baseline coarse-grained alloy. A clear falsification would be the absence of differential behavior between the two grain sizes under the defined testing temperature range.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach isolates the influence of mesoscale structural features (grain size and boundary effects) on the high-temperature mechanical and thermal properties, offering a direct controlled comparison that can be linked to stress–strain and expansion behavior.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction directly addresses the insufficient understanding of high‐temperature stress–strain, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior by probing the effect of short‐range order on dislocation behavior and thermal properties in the HfNbTaTiZr HEA.
critiques.constraints: It respects the material system and specified operating temperature range (673–1273 K) and uses established MD methods with validated EAM potentials.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound; the introduction of SRO altering local bonding and dislocation nucleation is supported by previous MD studies on HEAs.
critiques.feasibility: Large-scale MD simulations with >20 million atoms are challenging but feasible with high-performance computing resources and state‐of‐the-art potential models.
critiques.evidence: Prior MD simulation studies on similar HEAs (e.g. PMC4976365 and PMC11032334) support the influence of SRO on mechanical responses.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the imposed SRO might not significantly differ in its effect from inherent fluctuations in a random solid solution when simulated, compounded by uncertainties in potential parameterization.
critiques.fix: Calibrate the MD simulations rigorously by validating the chosen potential specific to HfNbTaTiZr and possibly include sensitivity analyses to quantify SRO effects.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction attempts to explain modifications in high‐temperature stress–strain behavior and thermal expansion by evaluating the role of deformation-induced defects, which can influence dislocation mobility.
critiques.constraints: It adheres to the material system and temperature constraints provided, though the use of a 20% cold roll might be on the lower side for inducing significant microstructural changes.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism invoking increased dislocation density and defect-assisted changes in mechanical response is physically plausible; however, the subtle degree of deformation may limit the observable effects.
critiques.feasibility: Experimental processing via cold rolling and partial annealing is well established, and the mechanical testing methods are standard.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from studies in similar HEAs (e.g. PMC7512503) shows that cold deformation can alter kinetic parameters and mechanical properties, though such changes may be muted at modest reductions.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that a 20% reduction might be insufficient to produce a strong microstructural signature or measurable difference relative to the as‐cast baseline.
critiques.fix: Increase the degree of cold deformation or optimize the annealing conditions to ensure a measurable and statistically significant change in dislocation density and defect structures.

critiques.addresses_problem: This approach addresses the open question by testing the influence of mesoscale features (grain size and boundary density) on stress–strain and thermal expansion behavior at high temperatures.
critiques.constraints: It respects the material system and operates within the specified temperature range (673–1273 K), though care must be taken to ensure other properties are not inadvertently compromised by extreme grain size alterations.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically reasonable, based on well-known effects of grain boundaries on dislocation mobility and thermal expansion modulation.
critiques.feasibility: Controlled grain size engineering via spark plasma sintering and subsequent heat treatments is an established route, though reproducibly achieving nanocrystalline structures in refractory HEAs can be challenging.
critiques.evidence: Literature on HEAs and similar refractory alloys (e.g. PMC7516662) lends support to grain-boundary effects on mechanical properties, despite differences in specific systems.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk lies in the experimental difficulty of reliably fabricating and characterizing uniform nanostructured samples without introducing unintended phase changes or residual stresses.
critiques.fix: Implement rigorous microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, EBSD) to confirm controlled grain size and ensure that any observed differences in mechanical behavior are solely due to grain boundary effects.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction directly targets the insufficient understanding by linking the degree of chemical SRO to changes in high‐temperature mechanical responses and thermal expansion.
critiques.constraints: It complies with the material system and temperature conditions (673–1273 K) while focusing on as‐cast alloys and feasible heat treatment protocols.
critiques.physical_soundness: The proposed mechanism is physically sound, as SRO is known to modify local bonding environments, affecting elastic moduli and dislocation mobility. This is consistent with studies on SRO in HEAs.
critiques.feasibility: Tailored heat treatments to control SRO are experimentally feasible, though ensuring reproducibility and quantification of SRO remains challenging.
critiques.evidence: Recent investigations (e.g. PMC11032334 and related records) support the influence of SRO on hardness, dislocation behavior, and hence overall mechanical properties.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is the difficulty in precisely controlling and characterizing the degree of SRO in as‐cast HEAs, potentially resulting in ambiguous correlations between processing and property changes.
critiques.fix: Integrate advanced microstructural characterization techniques (such as atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM) to quantitatively assess SRO and correlate it reliably with mechanical behavior.
